Message from the 
Presidents 


This past year has been tumultuous. An ongoing pandemic. Isolation. Inflation. 
Mental health. Humanitarian crises and conflicts. Academic struggles and 
increased school dropout rates. It seemed that as soon as we managed to 
wrap our heads around one challenge, another bigger one was right around 
the corner. And amid all this uncertainty, the only certainty was change. 


If the pandemic profoundly altered our world, changed our daily 
fitness routines, and exacerbated societal issues, it also showed us 
that change was not only inevitable but necessary. At the Y, we 
understood that to increase our social impact we needed to transform our 
business model and service offering to ensure our operational sustainability. 
In 2019, we began implementing our strategic plan, with an expected return 
to profitability by 2025. Now at the midway point in the process, we see how 
many of these changes are taking root and allowing us to better meet the 
growing needs of our communities. 


In 2022, we added a new investment fund to our long-term financial strategy. 
We invested in philanthropy and are extremely grateful to our donors who 
placed their trust and confidence in us. We reassessed our daycare model and 
made the difficult decision to close two sites. But we also built partnerships 

to take our programs and services outside our walls. Our integrated 
programming at the Olive-Urquhart Sports Centre, Pointe-Claire’s newly 
opened complex on the site of the former West Island YMCA, is one example. 


Nancy Audette 
Chair of the Board 
of Directors In 2022, we also amped up our efforts to support youth. We saw 
YMCAs of Québec record numbers of teens in our TeenZones. We expanded our 


Alternative Suspension program thanks to the social impact bonds 
Stéphane Vaillancourt and reopened Camp YMCA Kanawana after two years of closures. But 
President and CEO as we move forward, we need to make sure no one gets left behind. Our Social 
YMCAs of Québec Inclusion and Reintegration sector continues to focus on supporting some of 
the most vulnerable and marginalized populations. And the fully reopened 


Claudie Imbleau-Chagnon YMCA Residence provides housing and integration services to asylum seekers. 


President 
z = YMCAs of Québec Last, but certainly not least, we focused on taking better care of our 
| n cl U S i Oo n Foundation teams this year. Through an enhanced Employee Assistance Program that 


now also offers telemedicine, mental health workshops, and a new mentoring 
program, we want to ensure all employees have the support and 
res pect opportunities to grow both personally and professionally. Because without 
: them, none of the work we do would be possible. 
sO d a rity But there is still a lot of work to be done. Change is a process. One we 
would never have been able to start without the support and 
b Oo d Nn e SS generosity of our incredible donors, staff, members, volunteers, and 


partners. We hope that as you read through the pages of our impact report, 


Ca ri n you will be inspired and continue to support us in driving positive change in 
g the community. Because together, we can build a stronger tomorrow.

Strategic Plan 


In 2019, already aware that the organization 
needed to transform to better align with 

a constantly changing society, we set our 
transformation process in motion based on 
clear objectives and a well-defined 
strategic plan. 


The Y's Social Impact 


One of the driving forces behind our transformation is our desire to refocus and increase 

our social impact. The pandemic changed and exacerbated community needs. With a clearly 
defined impact model guiding our actions and decisions and a transformed, integrated, and 
sustainable business model, we will be able to meet those needs more effectively.

The YMCA Residence: 
A Warm Welcome 


Since 1984, the YMCA Residence has been offering 
housing services to asylum seekers. After being closed for 
almost two years because of the pandemic, the YMCA 
Residence reopened at the end of 2021. 


As the numbers of asylum seekers continues to rise 
in Québec, the Residence, in partnership with the 
Programme régional d'accueil et d'intégration des 
demandeurs d'asile (PRAIDA), plays a key role in 
welcoming newcomers. 


In addition to providing short-term housing and meals, 
residents can also take advantage of the winter clothing 
bank, a drop-in daycare service, and access to the YMCA’s 
sports and fitness activities, youth programs, and more. 
But most of all, the dedicated, caring staff ensures 
everyone gets a warm welcome as they have been 
doing for close to 40 years. 


In 2022, the YMCA Residence: 
- Housed over 1,000 people on average per day 
- Welcomed over 15,000 asylum seekers 
- Welcomed 18 kids per day on average in 
its drop-in daycare centre 
- Distributed over 600 items of winter clothing, 
including coats and boots

Manuel, Lead Syste: 
IT Department 


Manuel ’s Story 


Imagine trying to fit your entire life into two suitcases. That is exactly what Manuel and his wife did when they fled 
El Salvador in 2016 due to escalating violence and corruption. Like the tens of thousands fleeing El Salvador every year, 
the couple hoped to make a fresh start in a safer country. 


Upon their arrival in Montréal, they were housed at the YMCA Residence for several weeks. In addition to housing and 
meals, Manuel and his wife received help filling in all the paperwork for their asylum claim and guidance on services 
that would help them settle into their new life. “When | left the YMCA Residence, | was very well prepared thanks to all 
the help | received,” explains Manuel. Just two months later, he was enrolled in French classes, securing a job shortly 
thereafter. 


In 2020, Manuel's journey came full circle in a sense as he returned to the YMCA. Not as a stressed-out newcomer this 
time but rather as the IT Department's new lead system administrator. For him working at the Y is a way to “give back to 
society everything that was done for me.” 


DISCOVER HIS STORY: 
ymcaquebec.org 


Building for the Future |7 


A Journey Shaped by 
Societal 
Needs 


Beyond physical activity and sports, 
community and education have always 
been central to our mission. For over 

170 years, we have shown, time and 
again, our ability to transform and evolve 
based on the changing needs of our 
communities and the most pressing 
issues of our time. 


November 25, 1851 — North America’s first 
YMCA opens in Montréal. The Y has stayed 
true to its 1851 mission when it first began 
offering night classes to workers so they 
could build their “mind, body, and spirit.” 


1870 — Night school classes are offered 


to everyone, including women and 
immigrants. 


1890 — Ahead of its time, the Y begins 
to offer sports and physical activity as 
core components. 


1926 — The Y's night school leads to 
the foundation of Sir George Williams 
College (now Concordia University). 


8| Building for the Future 


1931 — Opening of the residence on 
Drummond Street to welcome the 
growing number of young men arriving 
in the city seeking employment and 
educational opportunities during 

the Depression. 


1960-1970 - The Y turns its focus to 
prevention and social intervention. Its staff 
pioneer frontline work by reaching out to 
young people struggling with addiction. 


1960-1970 — The Y offers its services to 
all Quebeckers, regardless of religion or 
language, to better meet the needs of the 
communities where it works. Previously, 
the YMCA only served English-speaking 
protestant men. 


1965 — Learning French becomes easier 
for immigrants with the opening of the 
accredited YMCA International Language 
School, which teaches nine languages. 


1969 — The Y launches host projects to 
integrate a burgeoning immigrant 
population. 


1970-1980 — To support working 
families and champion new ideas in 
child development, the Y opens daycares 
as well as preschool and after-school 
programs. 


1980-1990 — Responding to rising 
unemployment, the Y creates youth 
centres and employment services. 
Community development expands to 
include justice initiatives, minority rights, 
and urban development. The number of 
partnerships continues to grow. 


1984 —- The YMCA Residence begins to 
welcome refugee claimants. The YMCAs of 
Québec Foundation is also set up to ensure 
the Y’s future thanks to the generosity of 
donors. 


1999 — YMCA Alternative Suspension 
sharpens the Y’s focus on kids, youth and 
school success. It becomes a national 
program. 


2018 — Launch of the YMCA PlusOne 
Mentoring program, pairing caring 

and positive adult role models with 
10-to-17-year-olds who are experiencing 
challenges in their daily lives. 


2019 - Beginning of the Y’s 
organizational transformation process, 
with a greater focus on community 
programs and a recentred fitness 
programming. 


2019 — Official opening of the YMCA 
Saint-Roch thanks to a partnership with 
the City of Québec and the generous 
donors who helped equip the centre. 


2020 — The COVID-19 pandemic hits 
and the Y springs into action with virtual 
programs, online support, emergency 
services, and more. 


2021 — Launch of the YMCA Alternative 
Suspension Social Impact Bond, an 
innovative initiative aimed at funding the 
expansion of the prgram to 11 new 
service sites. 


2022 — The West Island YMCA becomes 

a Y Space thanks to a partnership with the 
City of Pointe-Claire. It offers sports and 
fitness activities as well as community and 
youth programs to area residents. 


Building for the Future |9 


| 
As part of our transformation, which aims to ensure our social impact for the long-term, 
we are reworking our business model, focusing on financial and operational agility. We are 
working hard on maximizing revenues from key sectors such as the YMCA International 
Language School and camps. We are adapting our health, fitness and aquatic programs to 
better meet the needs and changing behaviours of members. We are also looking to develop 
key partnerships for our centres, such as the one between the Saint-Roch YMCA and the City 
of Québec. 


In 2022, we refined our financial strategy launching an investment fund that would generate 
income to support our mission and operations for years to come. This strategic fund is financed 
by the sale of certain assets that are no longer financially viable and will complement our 
partnerships, philanthropic activities, and the diversification of independent revenue sources.

14| Building for the Future 


Sarah-Jeanne 
and Karolyn’s 
Steley 


Outgoing and bubbly, SarahJeanne is 
one of the Saint-Roch TeenZone’s first 
participants. For this Québec City youth, 
the YMCA TeenZone is a cool place to 
hang out with her friends and participate 
in a wide range of fun activities. 


As she loves to draw, the artistic 
workshops are really her favourite. 
But as youth worker Karolyn explains, 
TeenZones offer so much more than 
just activities. 


Sure, at the TeenZone, teens can do arts 
and crafts, play games and sports, go 

on a variety of group outings in the 
neighbourhood, or just chill with friends, 
but really the TeenZone is a place to 
connect. Connect with other teens whose 
reality may or may not resemble their YMCA TeenZones 
own. And connect with the youth 
workers, who, with time, become 
significant figures in the teen’s life— 
someone they can talk to about anything, 
from failing a math test to problems at 
home. Because bad days are inevitable, 
but friends and a good support network 
make them much more bearable. 


For youth to thrive, they not only need access to 
engaging and stimulating activities, but they also 
need positive environments and a stable, caring 
support network. But gaining a teen’s trust and 
building relationships is no easy feat and often 
requires patience, flexibility, and creativity. Enter 
the YMCA TeenZones. 


PUSSOC Ss ISS) 7 % ‘ YMCA TeenZones are safe, inclusive, and 
ymcaquebec.org /— f ae 

judgment-free spaces where participants can 
develop self-esteem and confidence. They are places 
of prevention. Places to build resilience, learn new 
skills, and have fun. Places to forge connections and 
build relationships. They are places where every 
teen belongs.

The YMCA Alternative Suspension 
Social Impact Bond 


Investing in the Generation of Tomorrow 

The YMCA Alternative Suspension Social Impact Bond 
(SIB) is an outcome-based financing agreement that 
aims to reduce the school dropout rate across Canada. 
This innovative funding approach, an initiative developed 
by Public Safety Canada and Impact Canada, relies on 
private investors to fund the expansion of the 
Alternative Suspension program to 11 new service 
sites, including four new sites in Québec. These 
investors, in turn, receive up to a 15% return on their 
investment from the Government of Canada based on 
the following metrics: 

* Participants’ change in behaviour 

« Program completion rates 


In the first year: 

- Investors received a 9.7% return on their investment 

« Program participants showed an average 24% decrease 
in negative behaviour after returning to school 


Led by the YMCAs of Québec, this is the first social 
finance project among all the YMCAs in Canada and 
involves numerous associations throughout the country. 


Thank you to some of our key investors including the Toronto 
Foundation, Inspirit Foundation, the Chawkers Foundation, Robert 
Kerr Foundation (Northwood Family Office), the Counselling 
Foundation of Canada, and Willow and Grace Foundation. Thank 
you to Scotiabank, who, thanks to a major donation through its 
ScotiaRISE™ initiative, catalyzed the YMCAs of Québec Foundation’s 
ability to invest in the YMCA Alternative Suspension SIB. These 
generous contributions mean hundreds of young people across 
Canada will have the opportunity to participate in the program 

and get back on the path of academic success.

“Dropping out of school is 
often precipitated by a negative 
event in a teen’s life that is 

hard to manage, such as a 
suspension from school. The 
YMCA Alternative Suspension 
program transforms a situation 
that interrupts academic 
progress into something 
positive.” 


Véronique Dupéré is full professor in the 
Psychoeducation Department at the University 
of Montréal, and, since 2021 has been on the 
Social Impact Bond committee.

The past few years showed us 
that it really does take a village. 


A village of committed and caring employees who 
worked tirelessly in difficult conditions to support our 
members, participants, and the community and offer 
them a place where everyone is welcome. 


A village of dedicated volunteers who gave their time 
and energy to help us bring our mission and impact 
to life. 


A village of members and partners who stayed committed 
to the YMCA and placed their trust in us. 


A village of donors who generously supported our programs, 
activities, services, and mission so we can all continue to make 
a real difference in our communities. 


We are so grateful that we could count on you when we 
needed you, and we are so proud that you are a part of our 
big YMCA family!

Volunteer 


2022 


To inspire each 
person to become 
the best version of 

themselves and 
actively contribute 

to their community, 
we work hard every 
day to offer a rich 
and dynamic 
organizational 
environment. 

Our boards of 
directors and 
committees are made 
up of committed 
volunteers who 
donate countless 
hours to giving back to 
their community, and 
our local advisory 
boards present an 
opportunity for 
members and local 
organizations to offer 
their perspective on 
local/community 
needs and contribute 
to our decision- 
making processes.
